messages.body_plain:
Hi Felix,

Thanks for the report, this is definitely a bug that should have been stopped. mixedmirt() objects don't really have a well defined information function in that each individual could have their own fixed/random intercept term. So the above model actually contains intercepts that are conditional on group, because logit(P) ~ aθ + d + beta * X, where X is the indicator variable for group. The problem gets even more complicated when beta is a random effect for groups, in which case information become much harder to define. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject: Fscores() and observations with only NAs
messages.subject_clean: Fscores() and observations with only NAs
messages.body_plain: I observed that when fscores() is called with argument full.scores=TRUE, values of factor scores (of about 0) are assigned also to observations that have no other value than NA on all variables used in the estimated model. It seems rather inconvenient to me. If regarding EAP or MAP estimators it can be justified as using only information from prior in absence of any new empirical information for these observations, fscores() behaves in the same manner also when ML or WLE estimator is selected. Generally I think that what most users would expected (analogously to most other IRT software) is assigning NAs to such observations (even if using EAP or MAP). Maybe at least a warning should be returned by fscores() if it detect such observations in the data.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: DIF and 3PL
messages.body_plain:
In theory a lot of this is fine, but for DIF it's better to free the latent mean and variance of the focal groups to adjust for overall group differences. You'll need to select a set of anchor items, set their parameters equal across groups, and add the invariance = c('free_means', 'free_var') argument to multipleGroup(). Try to follow the examples in help(DIF) because they properly set up the metric for DIF testing.

As for the code, I think it's okay. You are essentially performing a 2 df DIF test for the slope and intercept parameters and leaving the g parameters equal across groups (which makes sense, testing for DIF in the g's would require a massive sample size). My only issue is that, given your current sample size, the 3PL model will be pretty unstable and probably give bad estimates for the g parameters. I'd recommend either putting a strong prior on the g's, or simply set them all equal to some reasonable constant (like guess = 0.2, if there are 5 response options for each item, and then just use the itemtype = '2PL' argument). Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: A Question on Identifiability of Mirt models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I have been working a lot on identifiability of IRT models and how mirt handles identifiability. According to a seminal paper in my discipline (http://polmeth.wustl.edu/media/Paper/river03.pdf), IRT models are identified by imposing d*(d+1) independent restrictions on parameters, where d is the number of dimensions. So I have four sample cases of 2PL IRTs and would like to have your take on this:

1) One-dimensional mirt model is identified by setting latent mean to 0 and latent variance to 1, so it has 2 restrictions, and 1*(1+1)=2, so model is identified (up to a sign-shift)
2) 2-dimensional mirt model is identified by setting two latent means to zero, two latent variances to 1, and covariance between latent scores to 0, it has 5 restrictions, but 2(*2+1)=6, so the model should not be sufficiently identified although it runs in mirt by apparently setting one item parameter to 0 and hence satisfying identification restrictions, could you comment on this?
3) 3-dimensionanl mirt model where I fix three latent means and three latent variances, but want to estimate covariance freely is not identified in this form because 6<d*(d+1)
4) 2-dimensional mirt model where I constrain 7 out of 14 discrimination parameters per dimension to be zero should be identified with free variance, free covariance and free latent mean because 14>d(d+1).

I am especially not sure about the last one. Am I right here?

All the best,
Tobi

I had the same problem.  I used the mirt function mod2values and then wrote a little function using the reshape2 package function dcast.  This puts things in a dataframe.  the function acast would put it in an array.

Recast.m2v=function(df){
  tmp=mod2values(df)
  tmp=tmp[,c("item","name","value")]  #keeping just vars of interest
  tmp=tmp[1:(dim(tmp)[1]-2),] #stripping out group mean and cov
  tmp=tmp[tmp$name!="u",]  #all upperbounds of interest are 1 so this can be stripped too
  out=dcast(tmp,item~...)
  return(out)
}

messages.subject: missing levels in polytomous mirt: work around with a caveat
messages.subject_clean: missing levels in polytomous mirt: work around with a caveat
messages.body_plain:
If you are studying surveys with polytomous responses in samples that are not very large, it is to be expected that some item levels may not be observed.  This causes mirt to halt and burp out an error message.  I contacted Dr. Chalmers directly.  He suggested that I recode the data  so that no levels are missing.  This certainly works, but makes comparison of surveys were the level is missing with surveys where the level is present difficult.  I devised a work around which gives correct results.  HOWEVER, Dr. Chalmers points out that several diagnostic statistics will get confused by the dodge (see end of post).  Below you will find text of my exchange with Dr. Chalmers.

Hi Dr. Chalmers,

I have run into a problem using mirt, and I can't find a fix in the documentation.  I have thrashed around a bit and come up with something that might work.  So I am going to ask a long question which may have only a one word answer.

My colleague and I are trying to analyze a survey on student epistemic beliefs.  There are 14 questions (items).  All questions have potential responses of {1,2,3,4,5}.  This is a ordered agreement scale like a Likurt scale. My difficulty is that for some items, certain levels are not observed in the data set, and an error is generated when the mirt function is called:

> m.EB.1=mirt(EB,3,itemtype = "graded")
Error in FUN(newX[, i], ...) :
  Items contain category scoring spaces greater than 1.
                    Use apply(data, 2, table) to inspect and fix

If I add a dummy row of data to the data set so that all levels are present in the data set for all items, mirt runs fine.
>
> > dummyrw=c(1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1)
> > tst1=mirt(rbind(EB,dummyrw),3,itemtype="graded")
> Iteration: 254, Log-Lik: -1914.921, Max-Change: 0.00010
> > summary(tst1)
>
> Rotation:  oblimin
>
> Rotated factor loadings:
>
>               F_1    F_2    F_3    h2
> Innate_1    0.097  0.625  0.106 0.375
> Innate_4   -0.086  0.667  0.048 0.515
> Innate_7   -0.028  0.814 -0.133 0.665
> Innate_10  -0.134  0.647 -0.011 0.508
> Innate_13   0.062  0.764  0.111 0.582
> Explain_2  -0.004 -0.268  0.424 0.216
> Explain_5  -0.149  0.178  0.571 0.475
> Explain_8   0.199  0.009  0.717 0.484
> Explain_17 -0.237 -0.014  0.691 0.608
> Related_3  -0.799 -0.020 -0.029 0.616
> Related_6  -0.765  0.088  0.095 0.697
> Related_9  -0.626  0.249 -0.018 0.579
> Related_12 -0.723 -0.006 -0.010 0.516
> Related_18 -0.803 -0.092  0.018 0.598
>
> Rotated SS loadings:  2.942 2.681 1.55
>
> Factor correlations:
>
>        F_1    F_2    F_3
> F_1  1.000 -0.422 -0.246
> F_2 -0.422  1.000  0.154
> F_3 -0.246  0.154  1.000

Clearly, I have identified the problem, but I can't use this output, because my dataset is contaminated by the dummy row.

I need a mechanism to specify to mirt what the levels for the items are without influencing the estimate.  Thrashing around a bit, I devised a possible code script.  It runs, and gives plausible output.  I don't know if this is actually a valid way to solve this problem.

What I have done is to create an internal data set using the large=T argument.  I then manually changed the frequency of my dummyrow's data pattern to 0, and then reran the mirt using the altered internal data.  This runs, and gives factors that are distinct from the factors from the augmented data set.  Also, when I predict fscores, I get the correct number (125) rather than the 126 I get when I predict from the mirt on the augmented data without going through the frequency adjustment.  All of these are hopeful signs, but without knowing how the internal data is used in the mirt calculations I don't really know if what I have done is correct.

So here is my question.  Is this a workable approach?.

Thanks a bunch.
Dr. Chalmers reply to me below:

There are a couple of things to do here, but what I would recommend is to change all 1's in $Innate_10 to 2's; this will preserve the 1 space ordering, and will make mirt happy (and still treats the data are ordered, which seems to be the requirement here). Just keep in mind that doing things like fscores(mod, method = 'EAPsum') won't be too meaningful anymore, and fit statistics like the S_X2 that are based on the total scores are not invariant to the type of data transformation. Otherwise, if you don't care about those two stats, then all other methods should be invariant to transforming the data this way (ordinal is ordinal, whether it starts at 1 or 100).

This is a good question actually, and no doubt other will run into the same issue and wonder why mirt throws a seeminly odd warning. If you'd be so kind, would you mind forwarding this email to the google forum

Benny,

I can speak to the first question:

I don't believe there is any other information out there on how the MHRM algorithm performs when conducting DIF testing in MIRT models. I was not even aware of this article until you brought it up so thanks for that.  For what it is worth there is not a lot of literature on MIRT models and DIF in general at the present time although there is a recent paper on the LR tests albeit not with MHRM (e.g. Shu & Cho, 2014 doi: 10.1177/0146621614523116).

In the Asparouhov and Muthen article they used likelihood ratio (LR) tests and the BIC for the MHRM and they used IRTPRO which I believe Li Cai is not really doing much of any development on and instead he is now developing flexMIRT. In flexMIRT the DIF method they use is a variation on Lord's (1980) Wald chi-square test that has improvements. The biggest improvement was using the supplemental EM algorithm to estimate the SEs for the DIF tests. I think this test can be used for MIRT models in flexMIRT and if so the results from the Asparouhov and Muthen article might have been different (although you can't know for sure without a simulation) given what they found using Wald tests for the Mplus methods they compared with in the paper.

I mention all this because I believe Phil implemented the Wald chi-square test in a similar manner to what is in flexMIRT if you select the SE.type = "SEM" and run a DIF analysis in the multipleGroup function (I have not directly compared the results with flexMIRT as of yet but based on the documentation in the mirt package I think it is doing the same thing). What I don't know because I have not tried it is if this works on a mirt model in the mirt package (I assume it does but I have not personally tried it). If it does work and the Wald chi-square uses the SEM algorithm to estimate SEs I would consider using this test as it is much more computationally efficient compared with LR tests and is asymptotically equivalent to the LR tests.

To the best of my knowledge I don't think anyone has done a simulation study looking at the improved Wald chi-square with the SEM SE estimation in a MIRT model at this time. So I don't know what the performance of this test would be in the multidimensional case but in the unidimensional case it has performed quite well (see Woods, Cai, & Wang, 2013 for details doi: 10.1177/0013164412464875).

If anyone else wants to chime in on what I said please feel free.

Jared

Thanks Tobi, and sorry for the delayed reply (been busy in Europe). I see what you mean here, but I think this is somewhat specific for IRT models in that it really only is applicable to dichotomous tests. It's also not quite invariant in IRT models either because the expected theta values are computed by secondary means (unlike the glm example in the separationplot help files, where the expected values are fixed in the estimation algorithm). So you could get really different results depending on the estimator if the test size is small.

I think it's a neat example though, so I'll add a bit more to it in case others find it useful in the future. The predicted values are really just tracelines, so you could use the prodtrace() function built into mirt like so:

```

library(mirt)
library(separationplot)

data(SAT12)
#dichotomize
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5)
dicho.SAT12 <- key2binary(SAT12,key)
mirt_out <- mirt(dicho.SAT12,1)

#predicted values

fs <- fscores(mirt_out, full.scores=TRUE, scores.only=TRUE, method = 'ML')
holder <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dicho.SAT12),ncol=ncol(dicho.SAT12))

colnames(holder)<-colnames(dicho.SAT12)
for (i in 1:ncol(dicho.SAT12)){

    ii <- extract.item(mirt_out, i)
    holder[,i] <- probtrace(ii, fs)[,2L]

}

#PCP pooled over all items

mean(round(as.vector(holder)) == as.vector(dicho.SAT12), na.rm = TRUE)

#Separationplot over all items
separationplot(as.vector(holder), as.vector(dicho.SAT12), type='rect')
```

This will generalize a little nicer if 3PL items were used instead of 2PL. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: LL vs. information criteria from MHRM in nested models
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the late reply Benny, I've been busy with work in Europe. The MHRM is really hit with two forms of approximations: the estimation approximation (being stochastic in nature) and the approximation of the observed log-likelihood by Monte Carlo integration. So it's not a perfect system, and can give some funny results in likelihood ratio testing, so it's good that you are thinking about information statistics.

There isn't a lot of information on multidimensional DIF, even in the SEM literature (the topic is ripe for the picking, if you need publications). The reason I selected SABIC as the default criteria was that I too think the BIC is a bit restrictive for exploratory work (as DIF testing often is), so SABIC is slightly less so but still more than the AIC family.

mirt has tools to do both the Wald-type and likelihood ratio tests for DIF, though you are correct that Wald testing in these models has considerable advantages for higher dimensional models. I'm not sure how IRTPro of flexMIRT compute the information matrix though, but later versions of mirt run a separate section to try to make sure the information matrix is more stable (Cai's original publication on the method suggested that it could be built from the estimation history, but it turns out that's a very unstable approach). This is actually the approach I recommend in the mixedmirt() function anyways for mixed effects IRT parameter testing.

@Jared thanks for the reply, very helpful. You are correct that mirt has the supplemented-EM information matrix capabilities, which should be comparable to other software, but in this case it wouldn't be too useful. It's built on the (unaccelerated) EM history, so it really only works for 1-2 dimensional models. Anything higher is where the EM starts to break down, and where the S-EM would become very infeasible (besides, I have negative opinions about the algorithm anyway, as it is quite sensitive to many lower level tweaks and is very poor in small sample sizes....). Cheers.

Phil

On Mon, Feb 23, 2015 at 7:41 AM, Irshad Mujawar <irshadmuj...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Is there any limit ( upper and/or lower) on number of items for going together for calibration using mirt() function. What is the optimum number of items should one use at a time for calibration to get the best results?

I have no idea what this means. Optimal in what sense, measuring individuals precisely, item parameters or group parameters well; and what is meant be 'best' here? The smallest standard error (or a SE < #.... and for which parameters), the least bias, the most robust? The question is way too open ended to form a correct answer.

>
>
> Does this number change as we change the item type or ( dich or poly) or we change the number of dimensions underlying ?

Yes, and yes. More dimensions generally means that you need more items for everything, and polytomous items behave differently because they generally have more parameters to estimate (but also provide more information, so even that is difficult). But it also depends on the class of items: 1PL need far less subjects compared to the 3PL, and nominal many more than the gpcm. So the big answer to you email, and all statistical models in general, is that it depends on a large number of interacting factors.

Phil

mirt_sepplot <- function(x, type='rect', ...){
    require(separationplot)
    dat <- x@Data$data

    #predicted values
    fs <- fscores(x, full.scores=TRUE, scores.only=TRUE, ...)
    holder <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dat), ncol=ncol(dat))
    colnames(holder) <- colnames(dat)
    for (i in 1:ncol(dat)){

        ii <- extract.item(mirt_out, i)
        holder[,i] <- probtrace(ii, fs)[,2L]
    }

    #Separationplot over all items
    separationplot(as.vector(holder), as.vector(dat), type=type)
}

Each person was given a test, but the test was smaller for each individual than the total number of items, and therefore NA's should be used for items that were not observed. Now, you wish to pass these observed responses into a CAT? That doesn't make sense to me. What if an item is selected during the CAT where no observed response was realized (i.e., it turns out they have high ability, so a difficult item is selected, for which they originally did not respond to). Yes, but you'll have the same issue in Bayesian estimation. The posterior variance of the latent trait scores is not equal to the posterior variance term estimated in the model (you could easily verify that with something like MCMCpack).

> I initially thought I could easily exploit the fact that scores lie on the same metric to do further modelling, but especially variances of the empirical trait scores are quite different than 1, so this complicates things. Is there any way to impose the initial constraint (i.e. N~(0,1) used in the mirt-model fit onto the fscores() calculation of individual latent trait scores?

You might want to look into plausible value imputations, that seems to be what you are after. I don't suggest using point estimates for the factor scores, but rather draws from the posteriors and averaging over the secondary analyses using Rubin's methodology (see the ?averageMI function). Cheers.
